The methods, target treatments and search settings are retained. Peer data are published reports, not independently verified portal returns. See the dataset audit for exact sources and exclusions.

Function description and modelling clues¶

Course description, paraphrased. Tune two inputs to improve a noisy log-likelihood score. Multiple local peaks may occur; the objective is to maximise the returned score.

Source: Mini-lesson 12.8: function descriptions, reviewed 20 October 2026. The notes below interpret the fixed cohort snapshot collected on that date. Peer outputs are published reports, not independently verified portal returns. Every official objective remains maximisation of signed y.

Read the cohort evidence and exploration clues alongside these model results.

What the fitted comparisons add¶

The local GP has held-out MAE 0.1398, versus 0.2112 for the mean baseline. This supports useful predictive structure in this snapshot. Its conditional x2 slice predicts a dip between the upper and lower high regions, but that dip is a model hypothesis rather than a measured continuous profile.

The broad GP performs worse than the mean baseline. Smooth appearance alone therefore does not favour its explanation. The current UCB proposal, (0.595377, 0.993143), is outside the sampled hull; its mean 0.840 exceeds the best observation 0.611. That is explicit extrapolation, not a confirmed new peak. The assumed GP noise and latent-function bands do not measure the unknown repeat-evaluation noise described by the course.

Held-out comparisons and method selection use the same small snapshot; they are not independent final-test results. The notes do not change targets, settings or query policies.

2. Learn the picture before using it on the black box¶

The blue line is the GP's posterior mean: its central prediction after seeing observations. The pale band is mean plus or minus 1.96 standard deviations: a pointwise interval for the latent function under the model's assumptions. It is not a simultaneous guarantee for the whole curve, and it excludes fresh observation noise. Green crosses are measured values at the displayed inputs.

Only in this invented one-input example can we also draw the orange dashed known function. The three panels use 3, 6 and 10 points from a fixed invented sequence. They demonstrate updating a model, not a query-selection policy. None of these points uses the course query allowance. The GP's kernel, noise level and prior scale stay fixed across the panels.

The same visual convention is used in scikit-learn's introductory GP example. For the actual black box we have observations and predictions, but no known orange truth curve.

4. State competing models, then hide one result at a time¶

  • Mean baseline: ignore the inputs and predict the training outputs' average output.
  • Linear ridge: fit a tilted plane, with a penalty that restrains large coefficients.
  • Quadratic ridge: add x1**2, x1*x2 and x2**2, allowing broad curvature and an interaction.
  • Local GP: assume nearby inputs share information over an RBF length scale of 0.15.
  • Broad GP: repeat with length scale 0.35, sharing information over larger distances.

Both ridge penalties are fixed at alpha=1.0. The GP noise SD is assumed to be 10% of the training output SD. Targets are normalised inside each GP fit; feature scaling for ridge is also refitted inside each training fold. The GP settings are declared teaching assumptions, not fitted truths or the result of a hyperparameter search.

Leave-one-out (LOO) means each prediction hides its own observation and trains on the other 12. Lower MAE or RMSE is better. MAE / baseline < 1 beats the mean on this small-sample check. Training error shows how well a model represents points it has already seen; it is not the same evidence.

5. Repeat the prediction picture: vary x1, hold x2 fixed¶

Use the best observed input as a reference location. Vary x1 and hold its x2 coordinate fixed. This makes a one-dimensional slice through the two-input model. The left panel shows that path; its dotted boundary encloses the sampled inputs. The right repeats the blue mean, pale band and green measurements from the toy example.

Only measurements whose x2 actually matches the held value appear as green crosses on this curve. Other observations still influence the joint GP; they remain on the input map rather than being falsely projected onto the slice. The curve spans the full input interval, so parts outside the sampled boundary are extrapolations.

Use the local GP for this illustration; it is not automatically the best model in the validation table. A narrow band expresses this model's confidence, which can still be misplaced if its assumptions are wrong.

The three real-data curve pictures share vertical limits, so their apparent heights and band widths can be compared directly.

6. Repeat it again: vary x2, hold x1 fixed¶

Now move in the other input direction through the same reference point. The model and observations are unchanged; only the path through the input square changes. Read the same three elements again: mean, model band and measurements actually on the slice. Differences between the two curves describe the fitted input relationship, not a known property of the black box.

7. Change an assumption, then repeat the first slice¶

Return to varying x1, now with the broad GP. Its larger length scale shares information between more distant inputs. Compare the curve and band with Section 5 using their shared axis limits, then compare held-out errors in Section 4. The same observations can support different-looking predictions under different smoothness assumptions.

The GP band is conditional on its kernel and noise assumptions; it does not include uncertainty about which model is appropriate. Means can overshoot the observed output range. These unconstrained predictions do not establish that an unseen peak exists. The GaussianProcessRegressor documentation explains the noise parameter and returned standard deviation.

8. From curves to contour maps¶

A curve examined one path. A contour joins locations with the same fitted output y. Closer contour lines indicate a steeper change in the fitted mean; colours fill the bands between levels. These numbers are raw outputs, rather than observation ranks or uncertainty.

Predict the quadratic and local GP on the same input grid. Their panels share colour limits and contour levels. Coloured dots show measured outputs on that same scale; a dot differing from its background exposes a fitting mismatch. The gold star marks the best observed output. Blank regions are outside the sampled convex hull; interior gaps still have model uncertainty. Read these shapes alongside the held-out checks.

9. Separate a high prediction from high uncertainty¶

Read the next panels from left to right: the GP mean, its standard deviation, then an illustrative upper confidence bound:

$$\operatorname{UCB}(x) = \mu(x) + \kappa\sigma(x), \qquad \kappa = 1.96.$$

A high UCB can come from a promising mean, substantial uncertainty, or both. It is an acquisition score, not a predicted output or a guarantee of improvement. The weight is a declared heuristic. Its numerical agreement with the band multiplier does not prove an optimal policy.

Here the full input square is coloured so uncertainty outside the sampled hull is visible. The dotted outline marks that hull; coloured areas outside it are explicit extrapolations. Each panel has its own units and colour scale. The gold star remains the next saved coverage point, rather than a model-selected replacement. The table evaluates the remaining coverage inputs without changing their order.

10. If we switched today: a hypothetical model-led next query¶

Choose the lower-LOO-MAE GP among the two fixed GP comparisons, then maximise mean + 1.96 * SD over a declared finite candidate pool. A GP supplies both the mean and uncertainty needed for this rule; the lowest-error model overall may still be a different regressor. This is a transparent counterfactual policy, not proof that the GP or its settings are optimal. Selecting a model using these same 18 observations can make its reported error optimistic.

The pool contains 4,096 seeded Sobol points plus the four allowed extreme corners. Round inputs to six decimals before predicting, remove duplicates and already observed coordinates, then score those exact inputs. The winner is the best of this finite pool, not a proven continuous optimum. Candidates outside the sampled hull are permitted and explicitly labelled as extrapolations.

The table reports a single suggested input, its posterior mean, standard deviation and UCB in the model's target units. A second table changes only the exploration weight, reusing the same predictions. Weight zero chooses the highest mean. The magenta X marks the hypothetical query; the gold star remains the saved coverage choice. No new course evaluation is made, and the original Week 4 reference plan remains unchanged.

The chosen GP's MAE ratio is printed beside the suggestion. A ratio of 1 or more means it does not beat the mean baseline; the hypothetical query then lacks even that predictive support.

Read the pictures in the same order each time¶

  1. Identify the input path or plane, target scale and measured observations.
  2. Read the fitted mean before looking at its band or contour colours.
  3. Name the assumptions behind the uncertainty and check hidden-result errors against the mean baseline.
  4. Separate a predicted response from an acquisition score and the actual query policy.

The working evidence is a small comparison on 18 observations. Reusing these observations to choose among models can make the winning error optimistic. No picture supplies the unknown true surface or proves that a predicted optimum is real. For Week 4, the exploration notebook's coverage sequence remains the query decision; these model studies provide practice and hypotheses to revisit with future observations.
